levels.title: Translate a Business Concern into Data Questions
levels.objective: Use the translate a business concern into data questions technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: A useful analysis begins with a measurable decision question, population and time window. Worked example: A café manager says footfall feels lower but has only weekly receipts. The correct approach is to ask how many unique orders each day this week compares with the prior four weeks. Common errors include: report the number of social likes as proof of walk-ins or assume the decline is caused by rain without evidence.
levels.workedExample: Context: A café manager says footfall feels lower but has only weekly receipts. Applied technique: Ask how many unique orders each day this week compares with the prior four weeks.
levels.commonMistake: Report the number of social likes as proof of walk-ins
levels.remediation: Defined questions anchor the dataset and avoid speculative explanations.
levels.hint: Check that the action follows this data principle: A useful analysis begins with a measurable decision question, population and time window.

challenges.prompt: In "Translate a Business Concern into Data Questions", analyze this fictional business situation: A café manager says footfall feels lower but has only weekly receipts. Which approach supports a defensible conclusion?

options.a: Ask how many unique orders each day this week compares with the prior four weeks
options.b: Report the number of social likes as proof of walk-ins
options.c: Assume the decline is caused by rain without evidence

challenges.feedback: A useful analysis begins with a measurable decision question, population and time window. In this example, ask how many unique orders each day this week compares with the prior four weeks.

challenges.prompt: An analyst is helping a delivery shop evaluating more customer complaints. Which data step would produce the most defensible result?

options.a: Define whether the decision concerns complaint count, complaint rate or issue category and choose a fair time period
options.b: Treat the loudest single complaint as proof every delivery failed
options.c: Report social reactions as the number of resolved complaints

challenges.feedback: Define whether the decision concerns complaint count, complaint rate or issue category and choose a fair time period. Defined questions anchor the dataset and avoid speculative explanations.

challenges.prompt: Is this statement about "Translate a Business Concern into Data Questions" correct? A specific comparison question helps determine what data to collect before designing a chart.
challenges.feedback: Defined questions anchor the dataset and avoid speculative explanations.

levels.title: Define an Outcome Metric
levels.objective: Use the define an outcome metric technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: An outcome KPI measures a meaningful result rather than merely recording activity. Worked example: A tutoring business logs 150 new enquiries but knows nothing about registrations. The correct approach is to measure confirmed paid registrations divided by qualified enquiries alongside enquiry count. Common errors include: treat every enquiry as a paying customer or count message impressions as lesson completions.
levels.workedExample: Context: A tutoring business logs 150 new enquiries but knows nothing about registrations. Applied technique: Measure confirmed paid registrations divided by qualified enquiries alongside enquiry count.
levels.commonMistake: Treat every enquiry as a paying customer
levels.remediation: More enquiries may coexist with a lower paid conversion rate.
levels.hint: Check that the action follows this data principle: An outcome KPI measures a meaningful result rather than merely recording activity.

challenges.prompt: In "Define an Outcome Metric", analyze this fictional business situation: A tutoring business logs 150 new enquiries but knows nothing about registrations. Which approach supports a defensible conclusion?

options.a: Count message impressions as lesson completions
options.b: Measure confirmed paid registrations divided by qualified enquiries alongside enquiry count
options.c: Treat every enquiry as a paying customer

challenges.feedback: An outcome KPI measures a meaningful result rather than merely recording activity. In this example, measure confirmed paid registrations divided by qualified enquiries alongside enquiry count.

challenges.prompt: An analyst is helping a small brand reviewing how many leads became orders. Which data step would produce the most defensible result?

options.a: Treat every new lead as a completed paid order
options.b: Report follower count instead of lead-to-order conversion
options.c: Measure verified orders divided by qualified leads for the same reporting period

challenges.feedback: Measure verified orders divided by qualified leads for the same reporting period. More enquiries may coexist with a lower paid conversion rate.

challenges.prompt: Is this statement about "Define an Outcome Metric" correct? A larger enquiry count always proves conversion improved.
challenges.feedback: More enquiries may coexist with a lower paid conversion rate.

levels.title: Choose a Useful Comparison Period
levels.objective: Use the choose a useful comparison period technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: Time windows must be comparable and adjusted for weekends or seasonal changes where relevant. Worked example: A shop compares one Monday with a full six-day sales week. The correct approach is to compare like-for-like weeks or the same weekday and label the dates. Common errors include: declare sales rose because a six-day total exceeds a one-day total or ignore a holiday that affected hours.
levels.workedExample: Context: A shop compares one Monday with a full six-day sales week. Applied technique: Compare like-for-like weeks or the same weekday and label the dates.
levels.commonMistake: Declare sales rose because a six-day total exceeds a one-day total
levels.remediation: Use comparable periods and explain calendar differences.
levels.hint: Check that the action follows this data principle: Time windows must be comparable and adjusted for weekends or seasonal changes where relevant.

challenges.prompt: In "Choose a Useful Comparison Period", analyze this fictional business situation: A shop compares one Monday with a full six-day sales week. Which approach supports a defensible conclusion?

options.a: Declare sales rose because a six-day total exceeds a one-day total
options.b: Ignore a holiday that affected hours
options.c: Compare like-for-like weeks or the same weekday and label the dates

challenges.feedback: Time windows must be comparable and adjusted for weekends or seasonal changes where relevant. In this example, compare like-for-like weeks or the same weekday and label the dates.

options.a: Omit examination dates and claim attendance changes have one cause
options.b: Compare equivalent school days or weeks and explain the exam-period difference
options.c: Compare a full term with one afternoon without normalization

challenges.feedback: Compare equivalent school days or weeks and explain the exam-period difference. Use comparable periods and explain calendar differences.

challenges.feedback: Use comparable periods and explain calendar differences.

levels.title: Identify Missing Data Requirements
levels.objective: Use the identify missing data requirements technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: Document what is not recorded before asserting a conclusion from partial data. Worked example: A seller has order counts but not refund statuses and wants net revenue. The correct approach is to request paid amounts, refunds and cancellations before reporting net sales. Common errors include: multiply all order counts by a guessed average price or remove refunded orders without evidence.
levels.workedExample: Context: A seller has order counts but not refund statuses and wants net revenue. Applied technique: Request paid amounts, refunds and cancellations before reporting net sales.
levels.commonMistake: Multiply all order counts by a guessed average price
levels.remediation: Missing fields can change both totals and interpretations.
levels.hint: Check that the action follows this data principle: Document what is not recorded before asserting a conclusion from partial data.

challenges.prompt: In "Identify Missing Data Requirements", analyze this fictional business situation: A seller has order counts but not refund statuses and wants net revenue. Which approach supports a defensible conclusion?

options.a: Request paid amounts, refunds and cancellations before reporting net sales
options.b: Multiply all order counts by a guessed average price
options.c: Remove refunded orders without evidence

challenges.feedback: Document what is not recorded before asserting a conclusion from partial data. In this example, request paid amounts, refunds and cancellations before reporting net sales.

options.b: Claim all registered people attended without verification
options.c: Add a guessed number of walk-ins to the registration total

challenges.feedback: Distinguish registrations from confirmed attendance and request check-in records before estimating turnout. Missing fields can change both totals and interpretations.

levels.title: Avoid Vanity Metric Traps
levels.objective: Use the avoid vanity metric traps technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: Activity counts may be useful signals but must be tied to conversion or retention outcomes. Worked example: A creator gains 20,000 video views while website orders stay flat. The correct approach is to report views alongside qualified visits and actual orders rather than claiming revenue impact. Common errors include: state that every view is a sale or remove order data because views look impressive.
levels.workedExample: Context: A creator gains 20,000 video views while website orders stay flat. Applied technique: Report views alongside qualified visits and actual orders rather than claiming revenue impact.
levels.commonMistake: State that every view is a sale
levels.remediation: Reach is not equivalent to actual business value.
levels.hint: Check that the action follows this data principle: Activity counts may be useful signals but must be tied to conversion or retention outcomes.

options.a: Remove order data because views look impressive
options.b: Report views alongside qualified visits and actual orders rather than claiming revenue impact
options.c: State that every view is a sale

challenges.feedback: Activity counts may be useful signals but must be tied to conversion or retention outcomes. In this example, report views alongside qualified visits and actual orders rather than claiming revenue impact.

challenges.prompt: An analyst is helping a retail campaign reporting shares without purchases. Which data step would produce the most defensible result?

options.a: Assume that each shared post generated a completed sale
options.b: Hide order results because the engagement numbers look better
options.c: Report verified purchases or qualified visits alongside social shares and avoid revenue claims without sales evidence

challenges.feedback: Report verified purchases or qualified visits alongside social shares and avoid revenue claims without sales evidence. Reach is not equivalent to actual business value.

challenges.feedback: Reach is not equivalent to actual business value.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Write a KPI Brief
levels.objective: Use the checkpoint: write a kpi brief technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: A KPI brief specifies decision, metric definition, numerator, denominator, time window and owner. Worked example: A fictional online shop asks whether checkout improvements helped customers. The correct approach is to define checkout conversion as verified purchases divided by eligible sessions over comparable weeks. Common errors include: use the number of page designs made as the conversion metric or report a percentage without defining its denominator.
levels.workedExample: Context: A fictional online shop asks whether checkout improvements helped customers. Applied technique: Define checkout conversion as verified purchases divided by eligible sessions over comparable weeks.
levels.commonMistake: Use the number of page designs made as the conversion metric
levels.remediation: Ambiguous metric definitions lead to inconsistent reporting.
levels.hint: Check that the action follows this data principle: A KPI brief specifies decision, metric definition, numerator, denominator, time window and owner.

options.a: Use the number of page designs made as the conversion metric
options.b: Report a percentage without defining its denominator
options.c: Define checkout conversion as verified purchases divided by eligible sessions over comparable weeks

challenges.feedback: A KPI brief specifies decision, metric definition, numerator, denominator, time window and owner. In this example, define checkout conversion as verified purchases divided by eligible sessions over comparable weeks.

challenges.prompt: An analyst is helping a service business setting a weekly repeat-customer report. Which data step would produce the most defensible result?

options.a: Report a percentage without explaining the eligible population
options.b: Define repeat-customer count from unique customer identifiers, a seven-day period and an explicit denominator
options.c: Count every order as a different returning customer

challenges.feedback: Define repeat-customer count from unique customer identifiers, a seven-day period and an explicit denominator. Ambiguous metric definitions lead to inconsistent reporting.

levels.title: Distinguish Numeric and Text Data
levels.objective: Use the distinguish numeric and text data technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: Display formatting must not cause amounts or quantities to be stored as nonnumeric text. Worked example: A CSV includes price values 900 and "Rs 1,200" in the same column. The correct approach is to parse and validate monetary amounts as numbers while retaining PKR as a unit. Common errors include: add the text amounts by concatenating strings or delete every row containing the currency label.
levels.workedExample: Context: A CSV includes price values 900 and "Rs 1,200" in the same column. Applied technique: Parse and validate monetary amounts as numbers while retaining PKR as a unit.
levels.commonMistake: Add the text amounts by concatenating strings
levels.remediation: Text parsing and conversion must happen before aggregation.
levels.hint: Check that the action follows this data principle: Display formatting must not cause amounts or quantities to be stored as nonnumeric text.

challenges.prompt: In "Distinguish Numeric and Text Data", analyze this fictional business situation: A CSV includes price values 900 and "Rs 1,200" in the same column. Which approach supports a defensible conclusion?

options.a: Parse and validate monetary amounts as numbers while retaining PKR as a unit
options.b: Add the text amounts by concatenating strings
options.c: Delete every row containing the currency label

challenges.feedback: Display formatting must not cause amounts or quantities to be stored as nonnumeric text. In this example, parse and validate monetary amounts as numbers while retaining PKR as a unit.

challenges.prompt: An analyst is helping a shop preparing a dataset with quantities typed as words. Which data step would produce the most defensible result?

options.a: Convert verified written quantities into numeric fields and flag uncertain words for source review
options.b: Add the quantity strings as though they were numeric
options.c: Delete every record whose quantity was originally typed as words

challenges.feedback: Convert verified written quantities into numeric fields and flag uncertain words for source review. Text parsing and conversion must happen before aggregation.

levels.title: Identify Invalid Dates and Values
levels.objective: Use the identify invalid dates and values technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: Date formats, unit ranges and field constraints should be checked before analysis. Worked example: A monthly report includes February 31 and a negative parcel count. The correct approach is to flag both rows for source correction and document the exceptions. Common errors include: treat February 31 as a real date or change the negative count to zero without checking the source.
levels.workedExample: Context: A monthly report includes February 31 and a negative parcel count. Applied technique: Flag both rows for source correction and document the exceptions.
levels.commonMistake: Treat February 31 as a real date
levels.remediation: Source validation prevents error propagation.
levels.hint: Check that the action follows this data principle: Date formats, unit ranges and field constraints should be checked before analysis.

options.a: Change the negative count to zero without checking the source
options.b: Flag both rows for source correction and document the exceptions
options.c: Treat February 31 as a real date

challenges.feedback: Date formats, unit ranges and field constraints should be checked before analysis. In this example, flag both rows for source correction and document the exceptions.

options.a: Replace every invalid timestamp with today's date
options.b: Sort unparsed dates as ordinary alphabetic text and trust the order

challenges.feedback: Flag invalid or ambiguous timestamps and compare them with the clinic's original appointment register. Source validation prevents error propagation.

levels.title: Detect True Versus False Duplicates
levels.objective: Use the detect true versus false duplicates technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: Records with the same visible amount are not necessarily duplicate transactions. Worked example: Two orders have PKR 850 totals but distinct IDs and timestamps. The correct approach is to use stable order identifiers and audit source events before deleting either. Common errors include: delete one because the totals match or merge the orders under one invented customer ID.
levels.workedExample: Context: Two orders have PKR 850 totals but distinct IDs and timestamps. Applied technique: Use stable order identifiers and audit source events before deleting either.
levels.commonMistake: Delete one because the totals match
levels.remediation: A duplicate must be established from the business event and its key.
levels.hint: Check that the action follows this data principle: Records with the same visible amount are not necessarily duplicate transactions.

options.a: Delete one because the totals match

options.c: Use stable order identifiers and audit source events before deleting either

challenges.feedback: Records with the same visible amount are not necessarily duplicate transactions. In this example, use stable order identifiers and audit source events before deleting either.

levels.title: Check Outliers Against Sources
levels.objective: Use the check outliers against sources technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: Extreme values may be genuine events or errors and need investigation before exclusion. Worked example: Daily sales mostly sit near PKR 8,000 but one day reports PKR 80,000. The correct approach is to inspect that day's source transactions and note any promotion or data-entry error. Common errors include: delete the observation because it changes the average or assume the business grew tenfold permanently.
levels.workedExample: Context: Daily sales mostly sit near PKR 8,000 but one day reports PKR 80,000. Applied technique: Inspect that day's source transactions and note any promotion or data-entry error.
levels.commonMistake: Delete the observation because it changes the average
levels.remediation: Outliers may be important genuine events, so compare them to primary source records before deciding whether they are errors.
levels.hint: Check that the action follows this data principle: Extreme values may be genuine events or errors and need investigation before exclusion.

options.a: Inspect that day's source transactions and note any promotion or data-entry error
options.b: Delete the observation because it changes the average
options.c: Assume the business grew tenfold permanently

challenges.feedback: Extreme values may be genuine events or errors and need investigation before exclusion. In this example, inspect that day's source transactions and note any promotion or data-entry error.

options.a: Check the movement against the stock ledger and delivery documents before labeling it an outlier

levels.title: Reconcile Totals After Cleaning
levels.objective: Use the reconcile totals after cleaning technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: Data corrections need a before-and-after record count and control totals. Worked example: A sheet has 50 orders worth PKR 120,000 before removing suspected duplicates. The correct approach is to reconcile unique order IDs and verified amounts with the source ledger after cleaning. Common errors include: declare any lower total to be correct or hide removed rows to avoid questions.
levels.workedExample: Context: A sheet has 50 orders worth PKR 120,000 before removing suspected duplicates. Applied technique: Reconcile unique order IDs and verified amounts with the source ledger after cleaning.
levels.commonMistake: Declare any lower total to be correct
levels.remediation: Reconciliation reveals accidental record loss.
levels.hint: Check that the action follows this data principle: Data corrections need a before-and-after record count and control totals.

options.a: Hide removed rows to avoid questions
options.b: Reconcile unique order IDs and verified amounts with the source ledger after cleaning
options.c: Declare any lower total to be correct

challenges.feedback: Data corrections need a before-and-after record count and control totals. In this example, reconcile unique order IDs and verified amounts with the source ledger after cleaning.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Verify a Small Dataset
levels.objective: Use the checkpoint: verify a small dataset technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: A reliable cleaning report separates confirmed fixes, flagged exceptions and unchanged originals. Worked example: A synthetic twelve-row file has missing dates, repeated IDs and inconsistent price formats. The correct approach is to create an exception log, correct only confirmed records and reconcile totals against the source. Common errors include: fill every blank with today's date or publish a perfect completeness rate despite unresolved values.
levels.workedExample: Context: A synthetic twelve-row file has missing dates, repeated IDs and inconsistent price formats. Applied technique: Create an exception log, correct only confirmed records and reconcile totals against the source.
levels.commonMistake: Fill every blank with today's date
levels.remediation: Accuracy matters more than cosmetically complete cells.
levels.hint: Check that the action follows this data principle: A reliable cleaning report separates confirmed fixes, flagged exceptions and unchanged originals.

levels.title: Choose a Fair Comparison Chart
levels.objective: Use the choose a fair comparison chart technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: Use chart types that match the question and structure of the data. Worked example: A business wants to compare monthly orders across three service categories. Common errors include: use a pie chart with unlabeled slices for each month and category or use a decorative 3D chart that distorts proportions.

levels.commonMistake: Use a pie chart with unlabeled slices for each month and category
levels.remediation: A shared axis supports direct comparison.
levels.hint: Check that the action follows this data principle: Use chart types that match the question and structure of the data.

options.c: Use a decorative 3D chart that distorts proportions

levels.title: Label Axes and Units Clearly
levels.objective: Use the label axes and units clearly technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: A reader needs the metric name, unit, period and scale to interpret plotted values. Worked example: A dashboard chart shows 20, 30 and 40 without saying whether they mean rupees or customers. The correct approach is to label the vertical axis "Orders (count)" and show the reporting dates. Common errors include: assume readers know every unlabeled number or use the title "Performance" without identifying the KPI.
levels.workedExample: Context: A dashboard chart shows 20, 30 and 40 without saying whether they mean rupees or customers. Applied technique: Label the vertical axis "Orders (count)" and show the reporting dates.
levels.commonMistake: Assume readers know every unlabeled number
levels.remediation: Chart labels must identify the measure, unit, date range and scale so a reader can interpret the numbers accurately.
levels.hint: Check that the action follows this data principle: A reader needs the metric name, unit, period and scale to interpret plotted values.

levels.title: Compare Categories Without Distorting Scale
levels.objective: Use the compare categories without distorting scale technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: A truncated axis can exaggerate small differences in bar heights. Worked example: Store A recorded 98 sales and Store B recorded 100 in the same period. The correct approach is to use a zero baseline for bar lengths and disclose the two-unit difference. Common errors include: start the axis at 97 to make Store B look three times as tall or use unequal bar widths without explanation.
levels.workedExample: Context: Store A recorded 98 sales and Store B recorded 100 in the same period. Applied technique: Use a zero baseline for bar lengths and disclose the two-unit difference.
levels.commonMistake: Start the axis at 97 to make Store B look three times as tall
levels.remediation: If showing percentage changes, explain the baseline separately.
levels.hint: Check that the action follows this data principle: A truncated axis can exaggerate small differences in bar heights.

options.c: Use a zero baseline for bar lengths and disclose the two-unit difference

levels.title: Interpret a Trend with Context

levels.teaching: A chart can describe a pattern but cannot alone prove what caused it. The correct approach is to report the rise and note simultaneous changes as alternative explanations. Common errors include: claim the campaign caused every additional signup or delete other campaign dates from the timeline.

levels.commonMistake: Claim the campaign caused every additional signup
levels.remediation: Other changes may influence the outcome.

levels.title: Describe Limitations and Missing Drivers

levels.teaching: Honest reporting explains data gaps, sample size and unmeasured factors. Worked example: A survey of eight customers is presented as if it represents an entire city. levels.commonMistake: Present the result as a national estimate
levels.remediation: Limitations narrow the appropriate conclusion.

levels.title: Connect Charts to Accurate Source Tables
levels.objective: Use the connect charts to accurate source tables technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: Every displayed metric should be traceable to a defined source and calculation. Worked example: A dashboard claims 150 fulfilled orders but the source sheet shows 145 delivered and five cancelled. The correct approach is to recalculate fulfilled orders from delivered status and document the filter. Common errors include: keep 150 because it was the earlier displayed number or delete cancelled rows from the master sheet to match the chart.

levels.commonMistake: Keep 150 because it was the earlier displayed number
levels.remediation: Reproducibility is part of trust in analytics.

levels.title: Add Caveats to Summary Insights

levels.remediation: A concise caveat can materially change the decision.

levels.title: Capstone: Present an Operational Dashboard
levels.objective: Use the capstone: present an operational dashboard technique to make a traceable and proportionate data-informed decision in a real work task.
levels.teaching: A complete report needs clean source data, calculated KPIs, charts, caveats and decision-focused recommendations. Worked example: A synthetic 30-order dataset contains delivered, cancelled and pending orders over two weeks. The correct approach is to create a reproducible three-KPI dashboard with a data dictionary, two charts, audit notes and prioritized action. Common errors include: present a decorative chart without underlying calculations or hide exceptions to make the dashboard appear successful. Capstone task: analyze a twelve-row fictional bakery order dataset. Report delivered order count, delivered revenue in PKR and delivery completion rate with defined denominators. Present two honest, labeled charts, a reconciliation log and a 150-word decision memo with caveats. Apply the supplied self-review rubric before seeking human review.

levels.commonMistake: Present a decorative chart without underlying calculations
levels.remediation: Auditable methods make the recommendation repeatable.
